title: AI Literacy for Humans
outcome: Understand what language models actually do, get reliable work out of them, judge their output critically, and use them responsibly in a life and a job.

phases.name: How These Things Actually Work
phases.outcome: Explain what a language model does mechanically, well enough to predict where it will fail.

modules.name: Prediction, Not Thinking
modules.objective: Describe next-token prediction and what follows from it.
lessons: The whole mechanism in one sentence, then unpacked
Tokens: how text gets chopped up
Why it can write fluently about something it has wrong
What "it doesn't know anything" does and doesn't mean
The analogies that mislead, and why
practice: Predict the model's behaviour in eight situations
lab: Test three predictions about model behaviour
Three predictions, the actual outputs, and what you were wrong about

modules.name: Where the Behaviour Comes From
modules.objective: Explain how training shapes what a model says, including its biases and refusals.
lessons: Pre-training: reading most of the internet
Fine-tuning and why it answers instead of continuing
Human feedback and what gets rewarded
Where bias enters and why it isn't removable by wanting it gone
Cutoffs: the world after training stopped
practice: Trace eight behaviours back to a training cause
lab: Find and document three training-shaped behaviours
Three documented behaviours with your explanation of the training cause

modules.name: The Context Window
modules.objective: Understand what the model can see at any moment, and what it has lost.
lessons: Everything it knows right now is in front of it
Long conversations and what falls off the edge
Where in the context something sits, and why it matters
Memory features and what they actually do
practice: Diagnose eight context-related failures
lab: Map where one long conversation degraded
A conversation log annotated with where and why quality dropped

modules.name: The Settings That Change the Output
modules.objective: Use temperature, length and system instructions deliberately.
lessons: Why the same prompt gives different answers
System instructions versus what you type
Length limits and answers that stop mid-thought
Reasoning modes and what they cost you
practice: Choose settings for eight tasks
lab: Run the same task across settings and compare
A comparison table with your conclusion about which settings suit which task

modules.name: Different Models, Different Jobs
modules.objective: Choose between models on evidence rather than on which one you heard of.
lessons: Big, small, fast, cheap: the real trade-off
Benchmarks and what they don't tell you
Testing a model on your own work
Local models: what's actually possible on your machine
practice: Match seven tasks to a model choice
lab: Run your own model comparison on a real task
A comparison on your own examples, with a stated recommendation

phases.name: Getting Reliable Work Out of It
phases.outcome: Write prompts that produce consistent, usable output, and improve them systematically.

modules.name: The Anatomy of a Prompt
modules.objective: Build a prompt from its components rather than writing a wish.
lessons: Request versus prompt: the difference in the result
Saying what not to do, and when that backfires
Role prompting: when it helps and when it's theatre
practice: Rebuild eight vague prompts from components
lab: Build a prompt for a task you do weekly
A component-built prompt, tested three times, with the outputs compared

modules.name: Teaching by Example
modules.objective: Use examples to pin down behaviour that description alone can't.
lessons: Showing beats describing for format and tone
Choosing examples that cover the edges
How many examples, and when more stops helping
Examples that accidentally teach the wrong pattern
practice: Select the right examples for eight tasks
lab: Build an example set for a classification task
An example set plus before-and-after accuracy on your own test cases

modules.name: Getting Output You Can Use
modules.objective: Specify output format so the result feeds into whatever comes next.
lessons: Asking for a shape, not just content
Output you can paste straight into something else
practice: Specify output format for eight tasks
lab: Build a prompt whose output feeds a spreadsheet
A prompt producing pasteable structured output across ten test runs

modules.name: Making It Show Its Work
modules.objective: Get intermediate reasoning you can check, rather than an answer you must trust.
lessons: Asking for steps and why it changes the answer
Plausible reasoning that reaches a wrong answer
Breaking one hard task into several easy ones
Asking it to check its own answer, and the limits of that
practice: Add verifiable reasoning to eight prompts
lab: Solve a multi-step problem with checkable steps
A worked solution where you verified each step independently

modules.name: Improving a Prompt Systematically
modules.objective: Improve prompts with evidence instead of by fiddling.
lessons: Why the first prompt is rarely the best one
Changing one thing at a time
A test set of your own hard cases
Judging two outputs against a written rubric
Knowing when it's good enough to stop
practice: Diagnose and fix eight failing prompts
lab: Improve one prompt across three measured rounds
Three prompt versions with scores against a fixed test set and a written conclusion

phases.name: Judging What Comes Back
phases.outcome: Tell reliable output from confident nonsense, and verify without doing the whole job yourself.

modules.name: Fabrication
modules.objective: Recognise fabricated content and know which topics attract it.
lessons: Citations, sources and quotes that were never written
Numbers, dates and the confident specific figure
Prompting to reduce it, and why it never reaches zero
practice: Find the fabrication in eight outputs
lab: Fact-check a full AI-written piece
A checked piece with every claim marked verified, unverifiable or false

modules.name: Verifying Efficiently
modules.objective: Check output at a cost proportional to what being wrong would cost.
lessons: What are you actually risking if this is wrong
Spot-checking that finds errors rather than reassures
Checking against a source rather than against your memory
Asking a second model, and when that's circular
Building a check routine for work you repeat
practice: Design a verification approach for eight tasks
lab: Build a verification routine for a recurring task
A written routine with the time it costs and what it catches

modules.name: Bias in Practice
modules.objective: Detect biased output in real tasks, not just in principle.
lessons: Where bias shows up in ordinary work
Testing for it: same task, changed detail
Defaults that assume a particular person
Health, disability and the assumptions models carry
What you can and can't fix with prompting
practice: Design bias tests for seven tasks
lab: Run a bias test on a task that matters to you
A test with varied inputs, the outputs compared, and your conclusion

modules.name: Agreement and Flattery
modules.objective: Notice when a model is agreeing with you rather than answering you.
lessons: Why it tends to agree with the premise you gave it
Leading questions and the answer you fished for
Asking in a way that permits disagreement
Using it to argue against your own position
When you should not be asking a model at all
practice: Rewrite eight leading prompts as neutral ones
lab: Test one of your own beliefs against a model, properly
A record of a neutral test, what it said, and whether you changed your mind

modules.name: What It Cannot Do
modules.objective: State the current limits accurately enough to stop wasting effort on them.
lessons: Arithmetic, counting and the things it's oddly bad at
Current events, and knowing what it can't know
Tasks where being usually right is worthless
Judgement calls that are not yours to delegate
practice: Judge eight tasks as suitable or not
lab: Write your own limits document
A personal list of what you will and won't use a model for, with reasons

phases.name: Using It in Real Life
phases.outcome: Apply AI to writing, research, learning, decisions and admin — with real gains, honestly measured.

modules.name: Writing With It
modules.objective: Use AI to write faster without producing writing that sounds like nobody.
lessons: Drafting, editing and critique are three different asks
Feedback on your writing that's actually useful
Difficult emails and messages you're dreading
What you should still write yourself
practice: Improve seven pieces of your own writing
lab: Rewrite something real of yours, with the process logged
A before-and-after with a note on what the model improved and what it flattened

modules.name: Research and Summarising
modules.objective: Use AI to get through material faster without losing accuracy.
lessons: Summarising a document you provide, versus asking from memory
Reading enough of the original to catch a wrong summary
practice: Assess seven summaries against their sources
lab: Summarise a long real document and verify it
A summary with every claim traced to a location in the source

modules.name: Learning With It
modules.objective: Use AI as a study partner without offloading the understanding.
lessons: Explanations at the level you're actually at
Asking it to quiz you rather than tell you
The illusion of understanding a good explanation
Learning from an explanation that might be wrong
Using it on a foggy day without it doing the thinking
practice: Convert seven passive study asks into active ones
lab: Learn one topic using AI and prove you learned it
A written explanation of the topic in your own words, unaided

modules.name: Admin, Health and Life Logistics
modules.objective: Use AI for the paperwork and admin that chronic illness generates, safely.
lessons: Letters, appeals and forms you're too tired to write
Preparing for an appointment: questions and a summary
Understanding a document written to be hard to understand
What never to put in: your data, other people's data
Medical information: what it can help with and where to stop
practice: Judge seven personal-use scenarios for safety
lab: Draft one real piece of admin, with privacy handled
A usable draft plus a note on what you redacted and why

modules.name: Measuring Whether It Helped
modules.objective: Tell whether AI actually saved you time and effort, or just felt like it did.
lessons: Tasks where it's a clear win, tasks where it isn't
Energy cost as a separate measure from time
Dropping the uses that don't pay
practice: Evaluate seven of your own AI uses
lab: Measure two weeks of your own AI use
A log with time and energy for AI-assisted versus unassisted, and what you'll drop

phases.name: Ethics, Privacy and Power
phases.outcome: Understand who these systems serve, what they cost, and how to use them without harming yourself or others.

modules.name: What You're Sharing
modules.objective: Know where your prompts go and decide deliberately what to send.
lessons: Training on your data: policies, and reading them
Other people's data in your prompt
Health data and the specific risk
Redaction habits that don't cost you much
practice: Redact eight prompts appropriately
lab: Audit your own AI use for what you've shared
An audit with a written rule for what you'll send from now on

modules.name: Who Benefits and Who Doesn't
modules.objective: Assess the distribution of benefit and harm from AI honestly.
lessons: The work that got easier and the work that got worse
Whose labour is in the training data
Access: cost, language and who's left out
Disability: genuine access wins and genuine new barriers
practice: Analyse the distribution of effects in seven cases
lab: Write your own position, with evidence
A written position on AI's costs and benefits, with sources

modules.name: AI Making Decisions About People
modules.objective: Recognise and challenge automated decisions that affect real people's lives.
lessons: Where automated decisions already affect you
Hiring, screening and the filter you never see
Healthcare AI: what's real, what's marketing
Your rights to explanation and human review
practice: Identify the recourse in seven automated decisions
lab: Draft a challenge to an automated decision
A written challenge citing the specific right and the specific defect

modules.name: Disclosure and Honesty
modules.objective: Decide when to say AI was involved, and be able to justify the line you draw.
lessons: Where disclosure matters and where it's noise
Work, study and the rules you're actually under
Writing a disclosure that's honest and brief
practice: Decide the disclosure obligation in eight situations
lab: Write your own disclosure policy
A personal policy with the reasoning and three worked examples

modules.name: Dependence and Deskilling
modules.objective: Notice what you're losing the ability to do, and decide whether you mind.
lessons: Skills that atrophy when you stop using them
Which ones you actually want to keep
Working when the tool is down
Assistive dependence versus deskilling: not the same thing
Your own working agreement with these tools
practice: Classify seven dependencies as fine or not
lab: Spend a week measuring one dependency
A record of doing one AI-assisted task unaided, and what it cost

phases.name: Making Things With It
phases.outcome: Go beyond chatting — build small tools, automations and workflows powered by AI, and know what they cost.

modules.name: Beyond the Chat Box
modules.objective: Understand the ways AI gets embedded in software and which suit which job.
lessons: What an API call actually is
No-code and low-code AI tools, honestly assessed
When a script beats a conversation
Choosing the simplest thing that works
practice: Choose the right approach for seven ideas
lab: Design an AI-powered tool on paper
A one-page design naming approach, inputs, outputs and failure handling

modules.name: Small Automations That Pay Off
modules.objective: Automate a repetitive task of your own with AI in the loop.
lessons: Where the AI step belongs in the chain
What happens when a step fails
practice: Design seven automations with failure handling
lab: Build one automation you'll actually use
A working automation plus a two-week record of whether you kept using it

modules.name: What It Costs
modules.objective: Estimate and control what AI use costs in money and in time.
lessons: Tokens and how usage is billed
Estimating the cost of a workflow before you build it
Free tiers, limits and what happens at the wall
practice: Estimate the cost of seven workflows
lab: Cost one of your own workflows at scale
A cost model for 100 and 10,000 uses with the assumptions stated

modules.name: Your Own AI System
modules.objective: Assemble a personal set of prompts, tools and routines that survives a bad week.
lessons: A prompt library for the things you do repeatedly
practice: Turn seven recurring tasks into library entries
lab: Build your personal prompt library
A library of at least ten tested entries with notes on when to use each

modules.name: Capstone — Solve a Real Problem
modules.objective: Apply everything to one real problem of yours, and evaluate honestly whether it worked.
lessons: Designing the approach and the checks
Building it and testing on real cases
Writing up what you'd tell someone else
practice: Critique seven capstone designs including your own
lab: Deliver the capstone
A working solution, its verification approach, measured results and an honest write-up
